question: What is the primary underlying problem when a post-operative patient goes into shock?

options.A: Rapid healing of the surgical wound causing stress
options.B: Total failure of the patient's digestive system
options.C: A sudden spike in the patient's daily fluid intake
options.D: Inadequate oxygen and blood delivery to vital organs

explanation: Shock fundamentally means the circulatory system cannot supply enough oxygen and blood to keep vital organs working properly. [learn more](BMP120_U4_T5#BMP120_U4_T5_h1)

question: Why is early detection of shock so critical in the post-operative ward?

options.A: It completely eliminates the need for any future surgery
options.B: It guarantees the patient will never take pain medication
options.C: It reduces the cost of hospital meals for the patient
options.D: It prevents the progression to full circulatory collapse

explanation: Catching warning signs early allows the care team to treat the root cause before the body's systems completely shut down. [learn more](BMP120_U4_T5#BMP120_U4_T5_h1)

question: Which waste product builds up in the body when cells are forced to use anaerobic metabolism?
explanation: Without enough oxygen, cells produce lactic acid instead of energy, leading to a dangerous acidic state in the blood. [learn more](BMP120_U4_T5#BMP120_U4_T5_h2)

question: What happens inside a cell when it runs out of energy during prolonged shock?

options.A: The cell starts producing extra oxygen to save the surrounding tissue
options.B: Sodium and water flood inside, causing the cell to swell and burst
options.C: Cellular walls become completely impenetrable to all fluids
options.D: The cell creates a protective shell and goes into a deep sleep

explanation: Energy failure stops the pumps that regulate cell contents, letting water and sodium rush in until the cell bursts. [learn more](BMP120_U4_T5#BMP120_U4_T5_h2)

question: Which type of shock is directly caused by a massive loss of blood after surgery?
explanation: Hypovolemic shock happens when the volume of blood or fluid in the body drops too low to maintain pressure. [learn more](BMP120_U4_T5#BMP120_U4_T5_h3)

question: A post-operative patient develops a high fever, chills, and dangerously low blood pressure due to a severe wound infection. What type of shock is this?
explanation: Infections that overwhelm the body and cause widespread vasodilation result in septic shock. [learn more](BMP120_U4_T5#BMP120_U4_T5_h3)

question: What is often the very first vital sign change seen in a patient developing early shock?
explanation: The heart beats faster to compensate for falling pressure, making tachycardia an early warning sign of shock. [learn more](BMP120_U4_T5#BMP120_U4_T5_h4)

question: Why does a patient in early shock often have cold, pale skin?

options.A: The body redirects blood away from the skin to protect vital internal organs
options.B: Poor nutrition prevents the skin from producing its own body heat
options.C: Cool skin helps the body lower a high post-operative fever
options.D: Anesthetic gases freeze the outer layers of the skin during surgery

explanation: To keep the brain and heart supplied, blood vessels in the skin constrict, causing paleness and a cool touch. [learn more](BMP120_U4_T5#BMP120_U4_T5_h4)

question: Why are the legs of a patient in suspected shock often elevated slightly?

options.A: To prevent the patient from trying to climb out of bed
options.B: To stop swelling in the ankles caused by intravenous fluids
options.C: To help blood flow back toward the heart from the lower body
options.D: To make it easier for nurses to check the pedal pulses

explanation: Elevating the legs uses gravity to return pooled blood from the lower extremities back into central circulation. [learn more](BMP120_U4_T5#BMP120_U4_T5_h5)

question: Which of the following interventions should be avoided when caring for a patient experiencing shivering during shock?

options.A: Ensuring large-bore intravenous lines are open
options.D: Placing lightweight blankets over the body

explanation: Restraints are unnecessary and dangerous; instead, light blankets are used to stop shivering without restricting movement. [learn more](BMP120_U4_T5#BMP120_U4_T5_h5)

question: What is the primary purpose of administering vasopressors like norepinephrine during shock?

options.A: To constrict blood vessels and raise blood pressure
options.B: To lower the patient's heart rate to a normal rhythm
options.C: To thin the blood and prevent dangerous clots
options.D: To put the patient into a deep sleep for surgery

explanation: Vasopressors tighten widened blood vessels, which helps push blood pressure back up to safe levels. [learn more](BMP120_U4_T5#BMP120_U4_T5_h6)

question: When are blood products preferred over plain crystalloid intravenous fluids in post-operative shock?

options.A: When the patient refuses to drink water by mouth
options.B: When the shock is caused by severe acute blood loss
options.C: When the patient has a mild post-operative fever
options.D: When the hospital pharmacy runs out of normal saline

explanation: Crystalloids add volume, but if red blood cells have been lost, actual blood products are needed to carry oxygen. [learn more](BMP120_U4_T5#BMP120_U4_T5_h6)

question: What is considered the most reliable non-invasive indicator of adequate organ perfusion in a recovering shock patient?
explanation: The kidneys are very sensitive to low blood flow, making urine output a direct mirror of how well organs are being perfused. [learn more](BMP120_U4_T5#BMP120_U4_T5_h7)

question: Why must the care team monitor a recovering shock patient carefully for signs of fluid overload?

options.A: Rapid fluid resuscitation can overwhelm the heart and cause fluid in the lungs
options.B: Too much fluid causes the surgical incision to heal much too quickly
options.C: Excess fluids will instantly dissolve all the circulating blood platelets
options.D: Patients who receive IV fluids always develop a permanent kidney disease

explanation: Pumping large amounts of fluid into a recovering system can back up into the lungs, causing dangerous pulmonary edema. [learn more](BMP120_U4_T5#BMP120_U4_T5_h7)
